slides.title: What the compiler does
slides.main: What async turns into and why Pin.

captions: async fn becomes a state machine; let's see exactly which one
State machines, Pin, borrows, Send, async closures, async fn in traits, recursion, cancellation
Understanding this separates a confident async author from a beginner

slides.title: Desugaring
slides.main: Anonymous type; arguments move into the future.

captions: async fn f(x: u32) -> String ≈ fn f(x: u32) -> impl Future<Output = String> { async move { … } }
An async block's type is anonymous and unwritable; signatures say impl Future
Arguments move into the future: a reference parameter ties the future's lifetime to the argument

lines: fn f(x: u32) -> impl Future<Output = String> { async move { … } }

captions: The body is split at .await: a "before start" state, one per point, "done"
A state stores only variables live after the point; size is the largest set
poll starts at the current state, runs to the next point and returns Pending or Ready

lines: let a = f().await;   // a is alive after
let t = tmp();          // t does not live across .await

slides.title: Self-reference
slides.main: A reference into itself breaks on a move.

captions: buf = [0; 16]; let s = &buf[..]; x.await; — the slice points inside the same state machine
If the state machine is moved (into a vector, into a function), buf moves and s stays at the old place
Ordinary Rust cannot create self-referential values safely; async must, and the solution is Pin

slides.title: Pin and Unpin
slides.main: A promise not to move; Box::pin, pin!, Pin::new.

captions:
Pin

promises: the value won't be moved until destroyed; poll takes Pin<&mut Self>
Unpin means "may be moved even when pinned": almost all types are Unpin; an async block's state machine is not
Box::pin(f): on the heap; pin!(f): on the stack; Pin::new(&mut f): only for Unpin
Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + Send>> is so common that futures has an alias BoxFuture
select! and re-awaiting: pin the future with pin!, then poll it in a loop via .as_mut()
Projecting a future field in your own combinator: the pin-project crate, not hand-written unsafe

slides.title: Async closures
slides.main: A closure with an async block, real async closures, AsyncFn.

captions: |x| async move { x + 1 } is an ordinary closure returning a future; callable many times
Rust 1.85: async |x| x + 1 are real async closures; they work better with borrows
Traits AsyncFn, AsyncFnMut, AsyncFnOnce for generic functions over async callbacks

lines: let f = |x: u32| async move { x + 1 };
async fn apply(f: impl AsyncFn(u32) -> u32) -> u32 {

slides.title: Borrows
slides.main: spawn needs ownership: move and Arc.

captions: A reference may live across .await if the data outlives the future
tokio::spawn takes no references to the parent's locals: the parent would finish first
Pass ownership: move, Arc clones, channels: the most common beginner error

slides.title: Send
slides.main: Rc and MutexGuard make a future !Send.

captions: Rc, non-Sync references and MutexGuard living across .await make a future !Send; spawn won't compile
A std::sync::Mutex guard across .await: not Send and a deadlock risk
Release before .await (a block), tokio::sync::Mutex, or don't hold a lock while waiting
trait Source { async fn get(&self) -> u32; } — static dispatch
Not suitable for Box<dyn Source>: return a BoxFuture by hand
The async-trait crate does it automatically at the cost of an allocation; in generic code, Send bounds

lines: trait Source { async fn get(&self) -> u32; }

captions: async fn can't call itself directly: the state machine's size would include itself
Box the recursive call: Box::pin(fact(n - 1)).await
Big values across .await bloat the state machine: keep them on the heap; size_of_val; clippy::large_futures

lines: let buf = vec![0u8; 1_000_000];   // on the heap

captions: A future may be dropped at any .await: intermediate state in locals is lost
Example: part of the data is already read into a local buffer, the read is cancelled in select!: data lost
The language has no async Drop: cleanup that waits is an explicit close().await method or a separate task

lines: let n = rx.read(&mut buf).await?;   // part is in buf

captions: async block = state machine with states per .await; references inside → Pin; almost everything is Unpin except state machines
spawn: Send + 'static — ownership, Arc, move; std Mutex guard not across .await; recursion — Box::pin; code survives cancellation
